findings.issue_text: P1: Blocked-email blocklist is trivially bypassed via case variation — `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` in app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 is an exact case-sensitive match with no downcasing/normalization of either stored entries or checked values, and case-sensitive email uniqueness in user.rb:46 lets `SPAM@evil.com` and `spam@evil.com` coexist as distinct accounts

P2: Unanchored domain regex `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` in lib/validators/email_validator.rb:18-22 matches anywhere in the string, allowing whitelist bypass via suffix domains (e.g. `user@gmail.com.evil.com` delivers to attacker's MX) and blacklist bypass via subdomains (e.g. `user@sub.evil.com` doesn't match `@evil.com`)

P3: `Regexp.new` on raw admin setting in lib/validators/email_validator.rb:20 only escapes `.`, so regex metacharacters in email_domains_whitelist/blacklist (e.g. `+`, `(`, `*`) raise RegexpError at validation time causing 500s on every signup (UsersController#create only rescues ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid), or silently broaden/narrow matching

P3: Distinct blocked-email error message (`user.email.blocked`) in users_controller.rb:196-200 lets unauthenticated callers enumerate which specific addresses are blocklisted via POST /users, and every probe executes a SELECT + UPDATE (match_count/last_match_at), allowing anonymous users to inflate moderation telemetry and generate DB writes at will

P3: Non-atomic read-modify-write in `should_block?` (app/models/blocked_email.rb:14-16) — `record.match_count += 1; record.save` is not atomic so concurrent signups lose counter updates, and the return value of `save` is ignored so a failed write silently proceeds as if checked

P3: `validates :email, email: true` performs no format validation — `validate_each` in lib/validators/email_validator.rb only checks domain whitelist/blacklist and blocklist, accepting invalid values like `foo`, `a@b@c`, or `x@gmail.com@evil.com`, causing activation mail to bounce silently and enabling the embedded-@ whitelist bypass

New errors/values response fields carry no error-type discrimination, so the client conflates 'blocked' with every other email failure — duplicate-email validation errors ('has already been taken') flow into rejectedEmails, showing a wrong inline reason ('is invalid') and sticky false state that persists for the session even after the server-side condition resolves; server needs a typed signal (flag or error code) instead of relying on translated message text

BlockedEmail.should_block? performs DB writes (match_count increment, last_match_at update, record.save) from inside the validation chain, committing independently of the surrounding user.save outcome — increments are recorded even when signup fails, any bare valid? invocation silently writes to the DB, the predicate-named method is a trap for future callers, and record.save's failure return is silently ignored

Blocked-email matching is exact and case-sensitive with no normalization on write or read, so blocking spam@evil.com does not block Spam@evil.com, trivially evading the block and undermining the feature's core purpose as a moderation control

Unhandled DB write on the registration critical path: EmailValidator#validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which performs an UPDATE on blocked_emails as a side effect of validation with no rescue/retry; a DB failure (deadlock, statement timeout, dropped connection) propagates out of valid? and aborts an otherwise-valid signup, and concurrent UPDATEs serialize on the row lock under spam floods

Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count: match_count += 1 followed by record.save is not an atomic increment, so concurrent attempts with the same email lose increments; the boolean return of record.save is silently discarded on failure; and because the mutation fires on every valid? invocation, any flow that validates a user more than once double-increments the counter

Client blacklists the email on any server email error, masking the real reason: create_account_controller pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails whenever result.errors.email is present, but the server returns errors.email for every email validation failure (uniqueness 'has already been taken', domain whitelist/blacklist), not just blocking; once blacklisted, emailValid returns the generic 'is invalid' message contradicting the actual server reason and gates submission, leaving the user stuck with a wrong explanation

Blocked-email matching is exact, case-sensitive string equality: BlockedEmail.where(email: email) compares the raw submitted string with no downcasing/normalization on storage or lookup (and the uniqueness validation is likewise case-sensitive), so a blocked address is trivially bypassable by varying case; additionally, if the server does normalize the email, the echoed result.values.email won't match what the user typed and the client-side rejectedEmails.contains(email) check silently never fires

Validator spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block?, so both tests only verify that the validator's if statement reacts to the mock's return value rather than exercising the real DB lookup against a persisted BlockedEmail

The negative test in email_validator_spec is vacuous: with Mocha, if the validator never calls should_block? or calls it with different arguments, the unmatched stub yields nil/falsy, no error is added, and the test still passes

No integration test for the PR's core behavior: signup with a persisted blocked email failing validation, the user.email.blocked message actually appearing (the locale key is never asserted anywhere — a missing key would render 'translation missing' to users), and match_count incrementing through the real flow

The new controller response contract (errors: user.errors.to_hash and values: user.attributes.slice(...)) that create_account_controller.js depends on (result.errors.email truthy, result.values.email set) has no controller spec pinning the exact shape
JavaScript behavioral changes — the rejectedEmails state, the contains guard now preceding the authOptions ok-path, and the rejectedEmails.@each dependency on emailValid — ship with zero tests

Any email error (including 'has already been taken' or a blacklist rejection) pushes the email into rejectedEmails, disabling resubmission with a generic 'invalid' message for the rest of the session; this conflation and the persistence of rejectedEmails across modal re-opens are untested behavioral decisions

Whitelist/blacklist logic moved verbatim from User#email_validator into EmailValidator is untested in its new home; coverage depends entirely on legacy user_spec.rb tests exercising it indirectly, and the diff touches no user specs so the moved restriction behavior may now be uncovered
Case-sensitivity bypass: the blocked email lookup is an exact string match with no downcasing visible, so Bad@Spam.com likely bypasses a stored bad@spam.com — a trivial evasion of the feature
The record.errors[attribute].blank? guard branch is untested: the blocked check is skipped when another email error is present, so match stats aren't recorded for those cases
should_block? behavior with nil/blank email is untested — it should return falsy rather than raising

Email blocking in should_block? uses exact-match, case-sensitive comparison (BlockedEmail.where(email: email)) with no downcasing on either side, so a blocked evil@spam.com can sign up as Evil@Spam.com and bypass the block; the case-sensitive unique index also allows the same address to be block-listed multiple times in different cases, and this is inconsistent with the case-insensitive domain blacklist matching in email_validator.rb

match_count increment in should_block? uses a non-atomic read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1 then record.save), so concurrent signup attempts lose increments; should use update_all("match_count = match_count + 1")

The side-effecting DB write inside validate_each makes valid? non-idempotent — every validation pass (e.g., a valid? pre-check followed by save) increments match_count again, and the write fires on every changed-email validation anywhere in the app, not just signup
record.save's return value is ignored in should_block?, so a failed stats write is silent

action_type column is NOT NULL with no DB-level default; the :block default is enforced solely by the before_validation :set_defaults callback, so any write path bypassing AR validations (raw SQL seeding/bulk import, save(validate: false), manual INSERT) raises a NOT NULL violation

Client pushes email into rejectedEmails on any errors.email, including the 'has already been taken' uniqueness error, not just policy blocks; rejectedEmails is never cleared (only a full page reload resets it), so a user who hits a transient or recoverable email error cannot retry that address for the rest of the session and gets a misleading generic 'invalid' message instead of the server's specific error

Blocklist matching in BlockedEmail.should_block? uses exact-string case-sensitive equality with no normalization on either side, so case variants of blocked emails (e.g. SPAM@SPAMCLUB.COM) bypass the block entirely — inconsistent with the same validator's case-insensitive domain blacklist/whitelist regex, and there is no normalization contract between server validation and client comparison

should_block? performs a DB write from inside a validation: match_count += 1 is a racy read-modify-write with no locking that loses concurrent updates, the counter increments on validation attempts rather than actual blocks (inflating match_count/last_match_at), and record.save's return value is ignored with any exception propagating out of user validation and turning signup into a 500

Client rejectedEmails array is populated for any email validation error (including uniqueness 'has already been taken', not just blocked emails), is never cleared, and persists in the long-lived Ember singleton controller across modal close/reopen, so a user can be hard-stuck unable to submit a now-legitimate email until a full page reload

The @(domain) substring regex matches @domain as a bare substring: subdomains (foo@mail.evil.com) bypass the blacklist while suffixed domains (foo@mycompany.com.evil.com) incorrectly pass the whitelist — pre-existing code moved verbatim from user.rb but now anointed as the canonical email validator

New specs stub BlockedEmail.should_block? entirely and never exercise the real wiring (that validates :email, email: true on User resolves EmailValidator, runs with if: :email_changed?, and adds errors that fail the save) nor the moved whitelist/blacklist logic, so a wiring mistake would ship with a fully green test suite

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, email_in_restriction_setting? builds a regex from the raw SiteSetting string via `domains = setting.gsub('.', '\.')` and `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)`. This only escapes dots; other regex metacharacters in the admin-provided whitelist/blacklist (e.g., `(`, `*`, `+`, `[` or an unmatched `(`) can change matching semantics or raise `RegexpError` during validation. There is no rescue around this in the validator or UsersController#create (it only rescues ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid), so a bad setting can cause signup to 500. This behavior is directly present in the diff (moved into the new EmailValidator).

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, `User` switches to `validates :email, email: true` (custom `EmailValidator`). The new `EmailValidator#validate_each` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) only enforces domain whitelist/blacklist and `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and contains no syntax/format checks, so values like `foo` or `a@b@c` would not be rejected by this validator. Additionally, `email_in_restriction_setting?` uses `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` without anchoring to the end of the string, so an address like `x@gmail.com@evil.com` can match a whitelisted domain substring (embedded-@ bypass).

adjudication_records.issue_text: New errors/values response fields carry no error-type discrimination, so the client conflates 'blocked' with every other email failure — duplicate-email validation errors ('has already been taken') flow into rejectedEmails, showing a wrong inline reason ('is invalid') and sticky false state that persists for the session even after the server-side condition resolves; server needs a typed signal (flag or error code) instead of relying on translated message text

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, any server-side email error causes the submitted email to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` (`if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... pushObject(result.values.email) }`). Later, `emailValidation` treats any email in that list as invalid and returns `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, regardless of the actual server error (e.g., uniqueness "has already been taken" or `user.email.blocked`). Because `rejectedEmails` is never cleared, the same email becomes permanently rejected client-side for the lifetime of the controller, even if the server-side condition changes. The response’s `errors` hash has no typed discrimination used by the client to avoid this conflation.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `EmailValidator#validate_each` which calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). `should_block?` performs a side-effecting `record.save` that updates `match_count`/`last_match_at` (app/models/blocked_email.rb) during validation. There is no rescue/retry around this DB write, so any DB exception (e.g., deadlock/timeout/connection loss) would bubble out of `valid?`/validation and can abort signup even when the user record would otherwise be valid. The UPDATE also introduces row-level locking/serialization on the matched `blocked_emails` row under high concurrency.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count: match_count += 1 followed by record.save is not an atomic increment, so concurrent attempts with the same email lose increments; the boolean return of record.save is silently discarded on failure; and because the mutation fires on every valid? invocation, any flow that validates a user more than once double-increments the counter

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?` the code does a read/modify/write (`record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = ...; record.save`) which is not an atomic increment and can lose updates under concurrent signup attempts for the same email. The `record.save` result is ignored, so failures to persist stats are silently discarded. Also, this mutation is triggered from `EmailValidator#validate_each` on every validation run (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), so any flow that validates the same User/email multiple times can increment `match_count` multiple times for a single logical attempt.

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, any failed signup response that includes `result.errors.email` causes the entered email (`result.values.email`) to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` (lines added around `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... }`). The server change in users_controller.rb now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash`, so `errors.email` will be present for *any* email validation failure (e.g., uniqueness, domain not_allowed via EmailValidator, blocked). Once an email is in `rejectedEmails`, `emailValid` immediately fails with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, masking the specific server-side reason and preventing re-submission of that same email with the correct message.

It also notes related side effects, but the underlying bypass risk matches the golden comment.

adjudication.rationale: In `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`, both examples stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (`BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?).with(record.email).returns(...)`), so the validator spec only checks that `EmailValidator#validate_each` adds/doesn’t add an error based on the stubbed return value, not that it correctly consults a persisted `BlockedEmail` record via the real `should_block?` DB lookup. (There is separate coverage of the DB behavior in `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb`, but this particular spec does not exercise it.)

adjudication_records.issue_text: The negative test in email_validator_spec is vacuous: with Mocha, if the validator never calls should_block? or calls it with different arguments, the unmatched stub yields nil/falsy, no error is added, and the test still passes

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb the “doesn't add an error…” test uses `BlockedEmail.stubs(:should_block?).with(record.email).returns(false)` but does not assert the method is called. With Mocha, a `stubs` setup won’t fail if `should_block?` is never invoked, and an invocation with different args would return the default `nil` (falsy), leading to no error being added and the test still passing. This makes the negative test weak/vacuous for verifying the new `BlockedEmail.should_block?` integration in lib/validators/email_validator.rb.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new end-to-end behavior: a persisted BlockedEmail can cause User email validation to fail via the new EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) and the create action now returns structured errors/values (users_controller.rb). The JS then caches rejected emails and shows a generic invalid message. Tests added are unit-level only (email_validator_spec.rb stubs BlockedEmail.should_block?; blocked_email_spec.rb tests should_block? in isolation) and do not cover the real signup flow with an actual BlockedEmail record, nor do they assert that the new locale key user.email.blocked is exercised (server.en.yml). So the finding about missing an integration test for the core behavior is diff-grounded and actionable, but it’s not itself a defect in the code.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `UsersController#create` failure JSON to include `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`, and the Ember controller now branches on `result.errors.email` and `result.values.email` to cache rejected emails. The diff adds model/validator specs but no controller/request spec asserting this response shape, so the new client/server contract is unpinned by tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: JavaScript behavioral changes — the rejectedEmails state, the contains guard now preceding the authOptions ok-path, and the rejectedEmails.@each dependency on emailValid — ship with zero tests

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new, stateful client-side behavior in `create_account_controller.js`: a `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` array, an early `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` failure path in `emailValid`, and a new dependent key `('accountEmail', 'rejectedEmails.@each')`, plus mutation of `rejectedEmails` on failed signup responses (`pushObject(result.values.email)`). The PR adds only Ruby/model/validator specs and no JavaScript/controller tests covering these new branches or the ordering change (rejected email now fails before the `authOptions.email_valid` ok-path). This is a concrete, diff-grounded gap in test coverage for new nontrivial JS logic, not itself a proven runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Any email error (including 'has already been taken' or a blacklist rejection) pushes the email into rejectedEmails, disabling resubmission with a generic 'invalid' message for the rest of the session; this conflation and the persistence of rejectedEmails across modal re-opens are untested behavioral decisions

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a client-side cache of rejected emails: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` and an early failure in `emailValidation` when `rejectedEmails.contains(email)`, returning the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (create_account_controller.js). On account-creation failure it pushes the submitted email into this array whenever `result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values` (users_controller.rb now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: ...slice(...)`). This means any server-side email error (uniqueness, domain restrictions via `EmailValidator`, blocked email, etc.) will cause subsequent validations for that same email to short-circuit with a generic “invalid” reason, which is a nontrivial behavioral/UX decision and is not covered by any added tests in the diff. The claim about persistence across modal re-opens depends on controller lifecycle, which isn’t shown here, so that aspect is less directly verifiable from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Whitelist/blacklist logic moved verbatim from User#email_validator into EmailValidator is untested in its new home; coverage depends entirely on legacy user_spec.rb tests exercising it indirectly, and the diff touches no user specs so the moved restriction behavior may now be uncovered

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes `User#email_validator` (and its whitelist/blacklist checks) and reintroduces the same restriction logic inside `lib/validators/email_validator.rb#validate_each`. The newly added spec `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only covers the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch (via stubbing) and does not exercise the `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` / `email_domains_blacklist` paths. No user specs were updated in this diff to ensure those moved behaviors are still covered, so the restriction logic may now be untested in its new location.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Case-sensitivity bypass: the blocked email lookup is an exact string match with no downcasing visible, so Bad@Spam.com likely bypasses a stored bad@spam.com — a trivial evasion of the feature

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with the raw `email` value (no normalization/downcasing) and the model validation/index are on the literal `email` string (`validates :email, ... uniqueness: true` and `add_index :blocked_emails, :email, unique: true`). Nothing in the diff enforces case-insensitive matching, so a differently-cased input email can evade a stored blocked email on case-sensitive comparisons/collations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The record.errors[attribute].blank? guard branch is untested: the blocked check is skipped when another email error is present, so match stats aren't recorded for those cases

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the blocked-email path is guarded by `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, so when whitelist/blacklist adds an email error first, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is not called and match stats (`match_count`, `last_match_at`) won’t update. The new spec (`spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`) only covers cases where no prior email error exists, so this guard/skip behavior is indeed untested.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? behavior with nil/blank email is untested — it should return falsy rather than raising

adjudication.rationale: The diff’s `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` simply does `where(email: email).first` and returns `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`; passing `nil` or a blank string would not raise based on this code, and would evaluate falsy unless a matching DB row exists. The added specs don’t cover nil/blank, but the finding’s implication that this could raise is not supported by the shown implementation (and `EmailValidator` also guards by checking `record.errors[attribute].blank?` before calling `should_block?`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Email blocking in should_block? uses exact-match, case-sensitive comparison (BlockedEmail.where(email: email)) with no downcasing on either side, so a blocked evil@spam.com can sign up as Evil@Spam.com and bypass the block; the case-sensitive unique index also allows the same address to be block-listed multiple times in different cases, and this is inconsistent with the case-insensitive domain blacklist matching in email_validator.rb

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` the lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no normalization (`downcase`) on either the stored `blocked_emails.email` or the input `value` passed from `EmailValidator`. The migration adds a plain unique index on `:email`, which (on common DBs like Postgres) is case-sensitive, allowing multiple blocked rows differing only by case and allowing a user to bypass blocking by varying email case. This is also inconsistent with `email_in_restriction_setting?` using a case-insensitive regexp (`Regexp.new(..., true)`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: match_count increment in should_block? uses a non-atomic read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1 then record.save), so concurrent signup attempts lose increments; should use update_all("match_count = match_count + 1")

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, when a matching record exists it does `record.match_count += 1` and then `record.save` (read-modify-write). Under concurrent calls for the same email, this can drop increments because each request can read the same `match_count` and overwrite the other’s update. An atomic DB update (e.g., `update_all("match_count = match_count + 1")` or `increment_counter`) would avoid lost updates. This behavior is directly shown in the new `app/models/blocked_email.rb` code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The side-effecting DB write inside validate_each makes valid? non-idempotent — every validation pass (e.g., a valid? pre-check followed by save) increments match_count again, and the write fires on every changed-email validation anywhere in the app, not just signup

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value) whenever there are no prior email restriction errors. BlockedEmail.should_block? (app/models/blocked_email.rb) performs a DB write (increments match_count, sets last_match_at, saves) on every invocation. Since validations can run multiple times for the same operation (e.g., valid? then save, or other validation passes) and the validator is attached to User email changes (validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed? in app/models/user.rb), this makes validation non-idempotent and can inflate match_count/last_match_at updates outside of signup.

adjudication_records.issue_text: record.save's return value is ignored in should_block?, so a failed stats write is silent

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, when a record is found it increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and calls `record.save` but does not check the boolean return (nor use `save!`). If that save were to fail, the method would still proceed and return based on `record.action_type`, silently skipping the intended stats update. This is grounded in the diff (new `BlockedEmail` model) but it doesn’t break the primary blocking decision, so it’s more of a robustness/observability issue than a clear functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: action_type column is NOT NULL with no DB-level default; the :block default is enforced solely by the before_validation :set_defaults callback, so any write path bypassing AR validations (raw SQL seeding/bulk import, save(validate: false), manual INSERT) raises a NOT NULL violation

adjudication.rationale: The migration creates `blocked_emails.action_type` with `null: false` but no DB-level default (`db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb`). The model sets a default only via `before_validation :set_defaults` (`app/models/blocked_email.rb`), so inserts that bypass validations (e.g., `save(validate: false)` or raw SQL/seed inserts) can hit a NOT NULL constraint. This is a real, diff-grounded robustness/schema design issue, though not necessarily a bug in normal AR create paths.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client pushes email into rejectedEmails on any errors.email, including the 'has already been taken' uniqueness error, not just policy blocks; rejectedEmails is never cleared (only a full page reload resets it), so a user who hits a transient or recoverable email error cannot retry that address for the rest of the session and gets a misleading generic 'invalid' message instead of the server's specific error

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, on any signup failure where `result.errors.email` is present, the code unconditionally does `rejectedEmails.pushObject(result.values.email)` (no check for *which* email error). Later, `emailValidation` short-circuits: if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` it returns `{ failed: true, reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid') }`, and this list is never cleared anywhere in the diff. This means any email that ever triggered a server-side email error (including uniqueness `has already been taken` and the new `blocked` error) becomes permanently rejected for the session and will always show the generic “invalid” message instead of the server’s specific error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blocklist matching in BlockedEmail.should_block? uses exact-string case-sensitive equality with no normalization on either side, so case variants of blocked emails (e.g. SPAM@SPAMCLUB.COM) bypass the block entirely — inconsistent with the same validator's case-insensitive domain blacklist/whitelist regex, and there is no normalization contract between server validation and client comparison

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)`, lookup is `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`, which is an exact match with no case normalization. The new `EmailValidator` uses case-insensitive regex for domain allow/deny (`Regexp.new(..., true)`), so behavior is inconsistent: `SPAM@SPAMCLUB.COM` will not match a stored `spam@spamclub.com` row and will bypass blocking. The client-side `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` is also exact-string, with no normalization contract shown in the diff, reinforcing the mismatch.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_block? performs a DB write from inside a validation: match_count += 1 is a racy read-modify-write with no locking that loses concurrent updates, the counter increments on validation attempts rather than actual blocks (inflating match_count/last_match_at), and record.save's return value is ignored with any exception propagating out of user validation and turning signup into a 500

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#validate_each`, the new logic calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` during user validation. `should_block?` performs a DB write (`record.match_count += 1`, `record.last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`) with a read-modify-write increment and no locking/atomic update, so concurrent validations can lose increments/overwrite `last_match_at`. Also, `record.save`’s result is ignored (and only `ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid` is rescued in `UsersController#create`), so failures/exceptions here could affect signup flow. However, the “increments on validation attempts rather than actual blocks” looks intentional per the included spec (stats updated for both `:block` and `:do_nothing`), making this more of a design/concurrency concern than a clear functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Client rejectedEmails array is populated for any email validation error (including uniqueness 'has already been taken', not just blocked emails), is never cleared, and persists in the long-lived Ember singleton controller across modal close/reopen, so a user can be hard-stuck unable to submit a now-legitimate email until a full page reload

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, the failure handler pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` whenever `result.errors.email` is present (no filtering to only “blocked” errors). The email validation then hard-fails any future attempt using an email contained in `rejectedEmails` (`contains(email)` => `failed: true`). The diff shows no code path that ever clears `rejectedEmails`, so once an email hits any server-side validation error (e.g., uniqueness), that same email will be permanently rejected client-side for the lifetime of this controller instance.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The @(domain) substring regex matches @domain as a bare substring: subdomains (foo@mail.evil.com) bypass the blacklist while suffixed domains (foo@mycompany.com.evil.com) incorrectly pass the whitelist — pre-existing code moved verbatim from user.rb but now anointed as the canonical email validator
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same core flaw: the regex matches the domain as an unanchored substring (e.g., "@example.com"), so a whitelisted domain can be bypassed by using a subdomain like "evil.example.com". The candidate explicitly calls out subdomain bypass and lack of proper boundary/anchoring, aligning with the golden issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New specs stub BlockedEmail.should_block? entirely and never exercise the real wiring (that validates :email, email: true on User resolves EmailValidator, runs with if: :email_changed?, and adds errors that fail the save) nor the moved whitelist/blacklist logic, so a wiring mistake would ship with a fully green test suite

adjudication.rationale: The new validator is wired via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` in `app/models/user.rb`, and the whitelist/blacklist logic was moved into `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`. However, the only new validator spec (`spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`) calls `validate_each` directly and stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so it does not exercise the actual `User` validation wiring (resolver for `EmailValidator`, the `if: :email_changed?` condition, or that errors prevent a save) nor does it cover the moved whitelist/blacklist paths. That leaves room for a wiring/regression mistake to slip through with green tests, even though no concrete defect is shown in the diff itself.
